NEW DELHI: Israel on Monday wished India a happy Hindi Diwas , calling Hindi an "ancient language" that is "still very much alive today"."Two ancient languages, still very much alive today. Israel would like to wish everyone हिंदी दिवस की हार्दिक शुभकमनाएं!," Reuven Azar, Israel's ambassador to India, wrote on X.Union home minister Amit Shah on Monday extended heartfelt greetings to citizens on the occasion of Hindi Diwas, highlighting the role of the language in public communication, good governance and national integration, while calling for the empowerment of all Indian languages.In a post on X, HM Shah said, “Heartfelt greetings to all fellow citizens on Hindi Diwas. As the official language, Hindi is playing a vital role in strengthening public communication, good governance, and national integration.”“Hindi, which moves forward alongside all Indian languages, is now also becoming the language of technology and research. On the occasion of Official Language Day, I pay my respects to all the great personalities who have made an unforgettable contribution to enriching Hindi. Let us, on this occasion, resolve to empower all Indian languages, including Hindi,” he added.Defence minister Rajnath Singh also extended his greetings, describing Hindi as an important expression of India’s culture, civilisation and values.Singh posted on X, “Hindi is not merely a language, but a powerful expression of India’s culture, civilization, and life values. It is the language that weaves our diversity into the thread of unity. Enhancing the glory of Hindi is an act of honoring our rich linguistic and cultural heritage. Let us resolve to preserve, promote, and propagate Hindi, and make it even more robust in the fields of knowledge, science, technology, and innovation.Heartfelt greetings to all Hindi enthusiasts on Hindi Diwas.”Hindi Diwas is observed every year on September 14 to commemorate the adoption of Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union by the Constituent Assembly on September 14, 1949. The observance of Hindi Diwas began on September 14, 1953, and has continued since then.

Article Title: 'As India leads, world listens': Rajnath Singh hails 18th Brics joint declaration
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh Monday hailed New Delhi Brics declaration passed unanimosly, saying the unison adaptation was an "statement of India’s growing global influence" under Prime Minister Narendra Modi Calling "inclusive and human-centric approach" an hallmark of the summit, the defence minister laid emphasis on how the bloc put Global South "at the centre, not at the margins, championing a more inclusive, representative and balanced world order"."Rooted in our civilisational ethos of Vasudhaiv Kutumbkam, India has once again shown that leadership is not about having the loudest voice, but the strongest consensus," the Union minister said, adding: "As India leads, the world listens."In a dramatic echo of the 2023 G20 summit in New Delhi, Brics countries agreed on a joint declaration after intensive negotiations that continued until 4 am on Saturday. The talks were complicated by differences between Iran and the UAE over the West Asia conflict. An earlier meeting of Brics foreign ministers under India’s presidency had also ended without a joint statement.The 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi after a rare meeting between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit.The meeting took place as the conflict continued and helped ease the differences threatening consensus.The declaration used carefully balanced language to address the concerns of both countries. It expressed serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities operating under full International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, describing such actions as violations of international law and relevant IAEA resolutions. The wording amounted to an implicit criticism of US and Israeli strikes on Iran and was important in securing Tehran’s approval.The leaders also recalled their respective national positions on West Asia and stressed the need to maintain the smooth movement of global trade, supply chains and energy in line with international law.Official sources said India conducted prolonged negotiations at several levels to bridge the differences between Iran and the UAE. Other member-states also supported the effort, keen to ensure that the summit ended with a joint declaration rather than another failure to reach consensus.The agreement recalled the last-minute G20 declaration adopted in New Delhi in 2023 during the Russia-Ukraine war. That statement used carefully worded language urging countries not to use force to seize territory without directly naming Russia.

"in a dramatic echo of the 2023 g20 summit in new delhi, brics countries agreed on a joint declaration after intensive negotiations that continued until 4 am on saturday," he said. Talks were complicated by differences between iran and the uae over the west asia conflict.

Article Title: 'Prioritise national interest': Shashi Tharoor advises govt to keep Brics 'non-West'
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Shashi Tharoor on Friday cautioned that the Brics summit hosted by India should not appear to be an anti-West platform, as that would not be in sync with the country’s national interests.Tharoor, who served as a diplomat at the United Nations for decades, advised the government to showcase the concerns of the Global South while keeping India’s direct national interests in mind."As chair, we have a particular responsibility to showcase both the Brics as a forum, the concerns of the Global South in general, but also while bearing very, very carefully in mind our direct national interests. We want Brics to be a forum that is non-West, but not anti-West. That is exactly actually the same agenda as every other country. There are some others in Brics who are very happy to take it as a geopolitical non-Western, but also anti-Western platform," Tharoor told news agency PTI.He also said that PM Modi's scheduled meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping and the meeting with Russian president Vladimir Putin "are going to grab world headlines"."And I would like to say that that would not be in India's national interest...Becauseall these world leaders are in India, there will be significant bilateral conversations. Our Prime Minister is bound to be meeting each of the visiting heads of state and government who seeks a meeting. And that may mean a dozen important meetings with these country leaders. And for us, of course, both the meeting with President Xi and the meeting with President Putin are going to grab world headlines," the Thiruvananthapuram Lok Sabha MP said.Former Union minister Salman Khurshid also described the gathering as a “significant event” that allows India to demonstrate leadership on the global stage.Speaking to ANI, Khurshid stressed that the presence of leaders from all 11 member countries, including China, Iran, Russia, South Africa and India, could help New Delhi bring countries together, reduce contradictions and conflicts, and work towards creating better conditions in the world."This is a significant event. We hosted the G20 summit a few years ago, and the important thing is that the top leadership of China, Iran, Russia, South Africa, and India will all be present. All 11 countries will be present. It allows India to demonstrate leadership and ensure that contradictions and conflicts are reduced to a minimum. It can't be done overnight, but at least some attempt should be made. For India to have a locus as the leader and chairperson of the Brics summit, to be able to bring people together, converge, and accept positions that will create better conditions in the world," he said.Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said leaders from across the world would gather in New Delhi over the next few days for the Brics summit, expressing confidence that the high-level meeting would see positive and meaningful discussions on various issues with the welfare of the world in mind.“Over the next few days, leaders from around the world will gather for the Brics Summit. I am confident that the Summit will see positive and meaningful discussions on various issues with the welfare of the world in mind,” Modi said in a post on X in Hindi.The Prime Minister also shared a Sanskrit shlok highlighting the importance of cultivating relationships with virtuous people and promoting dialogue and goodwill.“A person should always live among the virtuous and cultivate their company. A person should engage in discussion and foster friendly relations with the virtuous, because mutual goodwill, dialogue and friendly relations strengthen peace and cooperation,” the verse said in a loose translation.As Brics chair in 2026, India will host the 18th Brics summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13. The summit will bring together leaders of Brics member and partner countries, as well as outreach invitees.During the summit, leaders are expected to discuss ways to strengthen intra-Brics cooperation on common priorities and exchange views on global and regional issues of mutual importance, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of External Affairs.Earlier on Thursday night, Bharat Mandapam, the venue for the summit in New Delhi, was being readied to host the high-profile gathering, with leaders and representatives from across the world expected to arrive for the September 12-13 event.
Article Summary: Shashi tharoor says govt must keep brics non-west and not let it appear anti-west. He also said that pm modi's scheduled meeting with chinese president xi jinping and the meeting with russian president vladimir putin "are going to grab world headlines" the summit will bring together leaders of brics member and partner countries, as well as outreach invitees.

Article Title: Xi's 5-point action plan for Brics may see red flags go up in India
Article Text:
Brics Summit 2026: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping

NEW DELHI: Chinese President Xi Jinping's statement on integrating markets and developing an open-source AI platform, along with other initiatives he proposed, is unlikely to enthuse policy circles here, given the wariness over such proposals from across the border.Ahead of China taking over presidency of Brics, Xi's speech at the concluding session of the summit is being seen as an indication that he would make a push for incorporation of these aspects into the agenda for next year's conference.For a long time, Brics has stayed away from becoming a trading bloc, and integrating markets through tariff cuts and investment protection regimes comes with the risk of opening markets to Chinese goods and companies with few guardrails, risking the development of homegrown technologies and players.India has maintained strict checks on Chinese investments, approving them on a case-by-case basis, and has refused to drop its guard despite the intense lobbying by sections of industry.The fear of Chinese cannibalisation of markets is not limited to India but is recognised globally - from Japan to Europe and the Americas - with countries trying to reduce their dependence and diversify sourcing. In fact, the rush of free trade agreements India has signed is partly driven by the strategy to diversify imports and govt's push to tap demand for Indian products through lower tariffs and reduced entry barriers.Ever since India walked out of RCEP in Nov 2019, fearing it would have to open the floodgates to Chinese imports, trade deals have become a crucial policy tool for India. It was China's dominance in RCEP that finally prompted India to opt out of the agreement, given that it had trade deals with countries such as Japan, South Korea and Asean members. Since then, India's portfolio has expanded to include FTAs with Australia, New Zealand, UAE, the UK, the EU and EFTA nations.The president's AI push in his five-point action plan, proposed Sunday, is among the biggest fears, given concerns about Chinese players and their development model. The push for Chinese LLMs, part of the proposals, is a sure-shot red flag and will be seen as an attempt to infiltrate countries amid global scrutiny of Chinese apps and technologies. India itself has blocked several apps and is on guard when it comes to allowing technologies in China-made cameras and other devices.Similarly, policymakers will be sceptical over the Chinese push for the SEZ initiative and the pitch to upgrade factories, especially when Belt and Road Initiative turned into a plan to corner key projects and use the funding to arm-twist governments into giving up control over the assets.
Article Summary: Chinese president xi jinping's statement on integrating markets and developing an open-source ai platform is unlikely to enthuse policy circles here. India has maintained strict checks on chinese investments, approving them on a case-by-case basis. The fear of chinese cannibalisation of markets is recognised globally - from japan to europe and the americas.

Article Title: 'Is it okay?' PM Modi pauses speech as Xi appears uncomfortable; Chinese president skips gala dinner
Article Text:

Modi, Xi discuss future of bilateral ties

Border, trade issues on agenda

Three ‘mutuals’ guide ties

Xi skips gala dinner

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly interrupted his opening remarks at the Brics Summit on Saturday after Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared to be uncomfortable.PM Modi turned towards Xi and asked the translator accompanying the Chinese president, “Is it okay?” He repeated the question moments later.It was not immediately clear what had caused Xi’s apparent discomfort. It may have been related to the microphone or the translation of PM Modi’s remarks. There was no immediate official reaction from China.The footage of the speech, shared by Doordarshan, shows the incident between the 4:30- and 5-minute marks. Xi, who was visiting India for the first time in seven years, later attended the Brics Summit and held bilateral talks with PM Modi.During their 40-minute meeting on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, the two leaders agreed that India and China should take a strategic and long-term view of their relationship and ensure that differences do not turn into disputes.Xi said the current momentum in bilateral ties, built on the resumption of institutional exchanges, an expanding cooperation agenda and growing trade, had been hard-won and should be cherished.PM Modi welcomed the “steady progress” in relations but underlined that peace and tranquillity in border areas would remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral ties.The meeting was the leaders’ third bilateral interaction in two years, following their meetings in Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin last year. It was also their first meeting on Indian soil in seven years.Xi reiterated that India and China were partners, not rivals. However, the Indian readout did not include that formulation.Also read: Why Xi Jinping skipped PM Modi’s gala dinner at Brics Summit in Delhi PM Modi stressed the need for both sides to honour existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues.The Indian side said the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to finding a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question, keeping in mind the broader political perspective of bilateral ties and the long-term interests of both countries.Modi also raised India’s trade deficit with China and called for greater predictability in supply chains and meaningful, predictable market access.The two sides discussed the need to address concerns related to structural trade imbalances, supply chains and economic cooperation.Since the 2024 Kazan meeting, which marked the end of the eastern Ladakh border standoff, three rounds of talks between the Special Representatives of India and China have taken place. At their latest meeting, the two sides agreed to work towards an early and substantial outcome on boundary delimitation and border management.The leaders also noted progress in people-to-people relations and stressed the need to promote cultural exchanges, business ties and greater mobility.“Prime Minister highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals- mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest,” the Indian readout said.They also agreed to expand common ground on regional and global issues and cooperate in addressing shared challenges.Xi called for a more rational and forward-looking strategic assessment of bilateral relations, win-win cooperation, mutual respect and understanding, and inclusive multilateral cooperation.Xi Jinping, however, did not attend a gala dinner hosted by PM Modi for Brics leaders, partner countries and representatives of international organisations, sources aware of the matter told PTI.The reason for his absence was not immediately known. A source suggested that Xi had returned to his hotel to rest after a busy day.Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, who left for home after attending the summit, was also absent from the dinner.Russian President Vladimir Putin and other Brics leaders attended the event. Union ministers, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and several chief ministers were also present.Union ministers at the dinner included Amit Shah, Nirmala Sitharaman, Piyush Goyal, Ashwini Vaishnaw and Shivraj Singh Chouhan. Chief ministers Yogi Adityanath, Devendra Fadnavis, Suvendu Adhikari and Himanta Biswa Sarma also attended.The ministers and chief ministers travelled in two buses from Parliament House to Bharat Mandapam, where the dinner was held.The dinner menu featured khandvi mille-feuille, khumb galouti, paneer lababdar, gucchi marmik, carrot-bean poriyal and millet pulao.The dessert menu included Old Delhi fruit cream with jalebi and shahtoot phirni. India is hosting the Brics Summit on September 12-13, with leaders from the 11 member countries and 10 partner countries, along with representatives of international organisations, attending the event.

Article Title: The Uranium rush: Inside India's scramble to fuel its nuclear ambitions
Article Text:

India’s nuclear math

Need for fuel

Thorium bet is the longer game

What’s next for India

Last month, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Tashkent, the headline takeaway was diplomatic. India and Uzbekistan agreed to elevate their ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and set a target of $5 billion in annual bilateral trade by 2030.But tucked into the joint statement was a line that could matter far more to India’s power planners than the trade target: the two countries agreed to work towards a long-term framework for uranium supplies.PM Modi had told delegates in Tashkent that India would "establish a long-term arrangement for the supply of uranium", describing it as the next step in the two countries' energy cooperation.It is easy to overlook why a single line on uranium in a joint statement matters.But it is perhaps the clearest sign yet of a scramble that has been building quietly across three continents, from Central Asia to Australia and North America, as India moves to secure the fuel needed for what could become one of the most ambitious nuclear expansion programmes of this century.Currently, the country operates 24 nuclear reactors with a combined capacity of about 8.78 gigawatts (GW).Centre's Nuclear Energy Mission, announced in the Union Budget for 2025-26, sets a target of 100 GW by 2047, more than an eleven-fold jump, with an intermediate goal of roughly 22 GW by 2031-32.That target, however, comes with a fuel problem.Industry estimates suggest a 100-GW fleet would require somewhere in the range of 18,000 to 20,000 tonnes of natural uranium a year, roughly a third of current global mine production.India's own uranium reserves, concentrated in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Meghalaya, are comparatively thin and have historically constrained, not enabled, the country's civil nuclear programme.For decades, that shortfall was managed quietly through a handful of government-to-government contracts.Now, with the expansion target locked in, it has become the organising logic behind a wave of overlapping diplomatic and commercial deals, of which the Uzbekistan framework is only the latest.India's relationship with Uzbekistan on uranium is not new. The two countries signed a contract back in January 2019 under which Uzbekistan's state-owned Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company agreed to supply 1,100 metric tonnes of natural uranium concentrate to India through 2026.Parliamentary records show India had received about 600 metric tonnes of that contracted volume as of March 2025, meaning the current arrangement was always going to need renewing, with expiry or no expiry.What changed in Tashkent was the structure.Rather than negotiate a one-off follow-on contract, the two sides are now working toward a long-term arrangement meant to outlast the transactional cycle of the 2019 deal.Siby George, secretary (west) in the ministry of external affairs, was quoted by news agency PTI as saying that "positive discussions have happened" on a long-term uranium supply arrangement, and that the two governments were "closing in" on signing it.No new uranium-specific pact was among the eleven agreements formally signed during the visit, the framework itself is still being finalised, but both governments used the summit to signal that Uzbekistan, one of the world's largest uranium producers, will remain a fixture of India's fuel-security plan rather than a legacy supplier being phased out.Earlier in July, India finalised the Administrative Arrangement with Australia under their 2014 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement.The arrangement, sealed at the Third India-Australia Annual Summit in Melbourne, operationalises a pact that paves the way for long-term Australian uranium exports to India under IAEA safeguards.Australia holds more than a third of the world's known uranium resources, by far the largest reserve base of any country, which makes the arrangement one of the more consequential fuel-security wins in India's recent diplomatic calendar.On the other side of the globe, India signed its most commercially concrete uranium deal yet, a nine-year, roughly $2.6-billion agreement between Canada's Saskatchewan-based Cameco Corporation and India's Department of Atomic Energy, for the supply of close to 22 million pounds of uranium ore concentrate between 2027 and 2035.The deal, signed earlier in March, was struck during a visit by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and both governments described it as a cornerstone of a new India-Canada strategic energy partnership.Separately, NTPC Ltd, India's largest power producer, tasked with building roughly 30 GW of the country's 100-GW nuclear target, has issued a tender to appoint consultants who will help identify uranium mining assets it could invest in overseas, in countries including Canada, Australia, Kazakhstan and South Africa.It is a telling move as state-run India is no longer content to simply buy uranium on long-term contracts. It wants equity exposure to the mines themselves.Together, the Uzbekistan, Australia and Canada threads are not three separate stories, but rather a larger picture of a nation that spent decades under-investing in fuel security and is now compensating for lost time on every continent that has the mineral.The external hunt for fuel has a mirror image at home: a domestic policy shift that is arguably even more consequential for India's energy sector.In December 2025, Parliament passed the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, ending a six-decade-old state monopoly over civil nuclear power generation.Under the new law, private companies can, for the first time, build, own and operate nuclear power plants, while the government retains control over the most sensitive parts of the chain — uranium enrichment, heavy-water production, and long-term spent-fuel management.The response from India Inc. has been immediate. A tender floated by state-run Nuclear Power Corporation of India for co-developing 220 MWe "Bharat Small Reactors" has drawn interest from Reliance Industries, Adani Power, Tata Power, Hindalco Industries, Jindal Steel and Power, and JSW Energy, a roll call of India's largest industrial conglomerates, each looking to secure captive, round-the-clock power for steel, cement and data-centre operations that a coal-fired grid increasingly cannot deliver cheaply or cleanly.Tata Power has gone furthest, publicly targeting 2032-33 for commissioning what would be India's first privately built nuclear plant, with construction beginning as early as 2028 across sites being scouted in Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Gujarat.The SHANTI Act creates the demand; Tashkent, Melbourne and Saskatchewan are where the supply is being lined up.There is another reason India's uranium scramble needs to be viewed as part of a much longer nuclear strategy.India has for decades pursued a three-stage nuclear programme designed ultimately to make greater use of its large thorium resources.The key transition is from today's uranium-fuelled reactors to fast breeder reactors and, eventually, reactors using uranium-233 produced from thorium.The Department of Atomic Energy describes thorium-232 as the material that can be converted into fissile uranium-233 for the third stage of the programme.That strategy reached an important milestone this year when the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu attained first criticality.The DAE describes the PFBR as the flagship of the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme and says thorium-232 can be converted into uranium-233 through transmutation, providing the fuel for the third stage.But the technology does not offer India an immediate escape from its uranium problem. The PFBR itself is part of a transition, while the large-scale nuclear expansion envisaged for 2047 still requires conventional reactors and therefore reliable access to uranium fuel.That explains the apparent contradiction at the heart of India's nuclear strategy: the country is rushing across the world for uranium today even as it develops technologies intended to make its nuclear fuel cycle more self-reliant tomorrow.The distinction matters because thorium is not a shortcut to the 100-GW target as it is a longer-term bet on the architecture of India's nuclear programme, while imported and domestically mined uranium will remain critical to the expansion now being planned.None of the deals struck so far, not Uzbekistan, not Australia, not Canada, comes close to closing the fuel gap that 100 GW by 2047 implies on its own.Each is best understood as one card in a hand India is still assembling: diversify suppliers, avoid dependence on any single country or company, and buy time for domestic reforms, the SHANTI Act, the Bharat Small Reactor programme, and a longer-term bet on thorium, of which India holds one of the world's largest reserves, to mature into an actual generation fleet.The Tashkent uranium framework, when it is finally signed, will not by itself power a single reactor.But it is a useful marker of how far India has travelled in eighteen months: from a country that mined and imported uranium exclusively through the state, to one running parallel negotiations with Central Asian suppliers, Australian miners and Canadian producers, while a queue of its largest private conglomerates waits for its first nuclear licence.The rush is real.Whether the fuel arrives fast enough to match India's reactor-building ambitions is the question the next few Budget cycles will have to answer.
Article Summary: India is securing uranium fuel for its ambitious nuclear expansion plans. India and uzbekistan agreed to elevate their ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership and set a target of $5 billion in annual bilateral trade by 2030. The two countries agreed to work towards a long-term framework for uranium supplies.

Article Title: Modi-Xi's Ukraine offer to Putin, strong message to West & new Brics playbook: Key outcomes of summit
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers opening remarks at the Brics Summit Session on 'Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth' at Bharat Mandapam, on Day 2 of the 18th BRICS Summit, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on Sunday. NEW DELHI: The 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi brought together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for two days of high-level diplomacy, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi holding key bilateral meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.The summit saw a renewed push to stabilise India-China ties, a reaffirmation of the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussions on the West Asia crisis, Ukraine, maritime security, trade and energy. Alongside formal negotiations, images of PM Modi with Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian projected a strong message of engagement and unity within the expanded grouping.The summit also featured informal diplomatic moments, including PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex, leaders attending a gala dinner featuring a specially curated Indian menu, and a symbolic Banyan tree plantation highlighting India's emphasis on sustainability and interconnectedness.The two-day summit also produced a series of initiatives covering agriculture, health, technology, startups, energy, urban mobility, supply chains, skilling and global governance. The New Delhi Declaration, adopted after intensive negotiations, provided the summit's principal political outcome, covering terrorism, conflicts, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.PM Modi and Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, with both leaders stressing the need to view India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.The two sides expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and said the relationship should be guided by mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The leaders also discussed maintaining peace and tranquillity along the border, economic and trade relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. Both sides underlined the need to address each other's concerns and facilitate meaningful and predictable market access.Also read: 'Have opportunity to discuss cooperation': PM Modi welcomes Xi; bilateral talks begin PM Modi also thanked China for its support and cooperation during India's Brics chairship and conveyed best wishes to China as it prepares to assume the Brics chairship next year.Xi said China and India should continue to approach their relationship from a strategic perspective and keep long-term bilateral development in mind. He also stressed the importance of cooperation between the two major Global South countries.PM Modi and Putin held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing major regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist peace efforts.Also read: Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeaways The discussions covered defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia also agreed to work towards increasing bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030 and discussed implementation of the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030.Putin invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, with dates to be finalised through diplomatic channels.One of the most closely watched visual moments came after the Modi-Putin meeting, when the two leaders travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The image underlined the longstanding India-Russia relationship at a time of continuing geopolitical tensions surrounding Moscow and highlighted India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.Also read: PM Modi, Putin share car ride again in Delhi, weeks after traveling together in Bishkek - watch PM Modi also presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.Russia said PM Modi and Xi offered their "good offices" to help find a solution to the Ukraine conflict during their separate interactions with Putin on the sidelines of the summit.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin welcomed their readiness, saying: “During their bilateral meetings, Modi and Xi took a keen interest in the Ukraine settlement and actively offered their good offices to help find a solution,”.The development came amid continuing international efforts to find a settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.PM Modi also met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the discussions focusing on India-Iran ties, Brics cooperation and the escalating conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's consistent position that disputes should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region. The two leaders also discussed freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers amid disruptions to shipping routes.The meeting followed their earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India has also stressed the need to expand and diversify bilateral trade channels with Iran.Pezeshkian also held talks with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on the sidelines of the summit.The meeting was significant as Iran and the UAE have had differences over regional security, while Gulf states maintain varying degrees of security cooperation with Western powers.Their interaction highlighted the diplomatic space created by Brics, which brings together countries with competing interests and positions on major geopolitical issues.The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals involving PM Modi, Xi, Putin and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, PM Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The visuals projected unity among members despite differences over conflicts and other major geopolitical issues.The interactions were particularly significant for India as it sought to use its Brics chairship to build consensus among countries with sharply different political and strategic priorities.Also read: PM doubles down on friendship with Iran, seeks win-win strategy; hope mounts for BRICS declaration Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner during the summit, providing an informal setting for interaction among heads of state and government.The specially curated Indian menu showcased regional flavours, traditional recipes and contemporary interpretations of Indian cuisine. The menu included Khandvi Mille-Feuille, Khumb Galouti, Paneer Lababdar, Gucchi Marmik, Carrot Bean Poriyal, Thakkali Belle Saaru, Millet Pulao, Beetroot Raita and assorted Indian breads.Desserts included Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi and Shahtoot Phirni.The cultural evening added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by negotiations over conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy and global governance.A symbolic Banyan tree plantation ceremony was also held during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the initiative.The Banyan tree, with its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".The plantation also reflected India's effort to connect the diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders for discussions on trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying Brics countries account for 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of global GDP and more than 25 per cent of global trade."The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date,” the Prime Minister said.Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing. Putin stressed that business-to-business ties and economic partnerships could help build more resilient international economic relations.India's chairship sought to connect Brics cooperation more directly with ordinary citizens while focusing on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.Addressing the summit, PM Modi said, "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach."He said resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability had remained India's priorities, with special emphasis on connecting Brics cooperation with common people."Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."India organised more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements across around 30 cities during its 2026 chairship. The programme covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.Brics countries advanced cooperation in sustainable agriculture through Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology, a Digital Agriculture Network and the Brics AGRIN framework covering agricultural inputs, genetic resources and information.The Digital Agriculture Network is intended to expand the use of AI, geospatial technology, Internet of Things-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics to support farmers.In healthcare, the Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle and a roadmap for joint cooperation on healthy lifestyles were launched. Members also agreed to strengthen cooperation in traditional, complementary and integrative medicine.A greater focus was placed on mental health through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India serving as the coordinating centre.Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The grouping also established a Brics Urban Mobility Hub to promote knowledge sharing and technical cooperation on sustainable urban transport. Members adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure and established an Urban Research and Knowledge Network.PM Modi also emphasised the importance of balancing development with environmental protection and said technology and critical minerals should not become instruments that hinder shared progress.India advanced cooperation among small businesses and startups through a Brics MSME Cooperation Portal designed to connect MSMEs, financial institutions, technology centres, trade associations and policymakers.The Brics Incubator Network will connect startups and incubators across member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.The Brics Science and Research Repository was also welcomed as a platform for scientific knowledge sharing.Through Brics CONNECT, members also advanced cooperation on skills, employability, women's workforce participation, social security and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation, while sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a dedicated working group.Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.Members also gave in-principle approval to an agreement on cooperation and mutual administrative assistance in customs matters, aimed at facilitating trade, reducing transaction costs and improving border security and trade facilitation.PM Modi used the summit to push for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making institutions.He argued that the Global South should move from being a rule-taker to a rule-shaper and called for reforms in global governance, including greater representation in the UN Security Council.Brics also reaffirmed support for comprehensive UN reform and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.The Brics countries adopted the New Delhi Declaration 2026, a 45-page document containing 140 points, after intensive negotiations that continued into the early hours of Saturday.The declaration brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.Its adoption was particularly significant because the expanded Brics includes countries with differing positions on major geopolitical conflicts, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. India worked to bridge differences and secure consensus among members.The declaration strongly condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and called for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemned the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemned the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards adopting the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.The declaration expressed deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stressed dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and called for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for upholding a ceasefire, ensuring unhindered humanitarian assistance and ending the forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.The declaration condemned unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts in West Asia and the wider divisions within the expanded grouping.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to reconcile competing positions and produce a common statement.Brics expressed concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.The grouping reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and called for restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.Brics also voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter, calling for such measures to be eliminated.The declaration backed efforts to promote cross-border payments and trade settlements using Brics members' local currencies while respecting national priorities.Members acknowledged work on the interoperability of payment and messaging systems and discussions on facilitating trade settlements and investment using local currencies.The push forms part of a broader effort to strengthen financial resilience and reduce vulnerabilities in international economic relations.The declaration stressed the importance of reliable, diversified, resilient and sustainable supply chains for critical minerals.It called for benefit sharing, value addition and economic diversification in resource-rich countries while recognising their sovereign rights over mineral resources.Brics also stressed the importance of critical minerals for zero and low-emission technologies, energy security and resilient energy supply chains.On energy, the declaration called for diversified sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets. It recognised that fossil fuels would continue to play an important role, particularly for emerging and developing economies, while backing equitable and inclusive energy transitions.The declaration reaffirmed Brics' commitment to universal health coverage and resilient, inclusive and people-centred health systems.Members emphasised the coordinating role of the World Health Organisation and backed continued multilateral cooperation on global health.The declaration also covered the Pandemic Agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing negotiations, efforts to end tuberculosis, strengthening the health workforce, digital health and integration of traditional medicine.Brics recognised women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.The declaration stressed women's participation in governance and economic life, financial and digital inclusion, skill development, entrepreneurship and climate action.The grouping also reaffirmed the importance of reforming global institutions to reflect contemporary economic and political realities and strengthen the voice of developing countries.The New Delhi Summit came as Brics entered its third decade with 11 full members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.India's 2026 chairship was its fourth after previous presidencies in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The latest chairship sought to build on those earlier efforts while adapting the grouping's agenda to its expanded membership.In his concluding remarks, PM Modi said the discussions had strengthened the view that Brics had evolved beyond a traditional grouping and could function as an ecosystem for practical solutions."Our discussions over the past two days have further strengthened our conviction that BRICS is not merely a grouping of nations, but an ecosystem of solutions. We hope that the New Delhi Declaration adopted at this summit will provide a clear direction for our shared vision and future cooperation. We must translate all outcomes into time-bound actions that deliver last-mile impact. We will work together to ensure that our framework moves beyond mere documentation and creates a tangible impact in real life," he said.PM Modi also said the world now expected concrete results from Brics rather than only ideas and commitments, as the grouping prepares to enter its third decade.
Article Summary: The 18th brics summit in new delhi brought together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for two days of high-level diplomacy. Prime minister narendra modi held key bilateral meetings with chinese president xi jinping, russian president vladimir putin and iranian president masoud pezeshkian.

Article Title: Altitude and attitude: How DGCA makes sure high-flying pilots don’t fly high
Article Text:
How India’s aviation regulator is tightening the net on pilots and crew to ensure those trusted with thousands of lives are fit to fly. (AI-generated image)

AAIB preliminary report

What happens when a pilot gets tested for drugs?

Crew perspective

The net gets wider

There is something inherently unsettling about flying. Thirty thousand feet above the ground, hundreds of passengers sit inside a pressurised metal tube travelling at hundreds of kilometres per hour, trusting a handful of people with their lives for the duration of the journey. Yet every day, millions of us make this decision without thinking twice.And then, once in a blue moon, an incident happens that makes us pause and wonder just how much we can actually trust those handful of people.On August 4, an Air India A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi was cruising at 36,000 feet when it suddenly climbed 372 feet before dropping nearly 300 feet. Twenty-four people on board, including passengers and crew, were injured badly enough to require hospitalisation. Twenty were discharged shortly afterwards, while four sustained serious injuries and remained hospitalised for further treatment. Many passengers also took to social media and spoke to news reporters about how frightening the experience had been.A preliminary report shows that, over those eight seconds, the aircraft lost all three of its hydraulic systems and the autopilot disengaged. The hydraulic systems recovered within seconds, and the aircraft subsequently landed normally.On the surface, it was a technical failure. But a second finding in the incident became the headline across news outlets.As part of the standard procedure following such incidents, the crew is tested on various parameters to ensure that investigators have a complete picture of what happened. In this case, both pilots underwent the mandatory psychoactive-substance test after arriving in Delhi, a requirement for flights originating outside India.The co-pilot’s sample came back negative twice. The pilot-in-command’s report, however, raised concerns. The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau’s (AAIB) preliminary report used the term ‘non-negative’ to describe both the screening test and the confirmatory laboratory report.What was reported as ‘positive’ in headlines was not, in fact, the language used in the report. In aviation investigations, that distinction matters. The AAIB’s responsibility is not to point fingers, but to establish what happened and identify measures that can prevent a recurrence.The preliminary report does not conclude that substance use caused the hydraulic failure. It does, however, flag a serious concern regarding psychoactive substances and recommends that the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) take appropriate action.The DGCA is the apex regulatory body responsible for overseeing safety standards in civil aviation. Its rulebook is extensive and is regularly revised to address emerging risks and ensure that flying remains safe for passengers and crew.Alcohol testing has been mandatory since the mid-2000s. The framework was built around Rule 24 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which originally required that crew members not consume alcohol within 12 hours of a flight. The rule has since been revised several times. A 2023 revision, for instance, warned that medicines and other substances containing alcohol could trigger a breathalyser reading, specifically citing products such as mouthwash and tooth gel. Crew members taking medication are required to consult their company doctor before flying.For scheduled operators, flight and cabin crew are subject to pre-flight breathalyser testing at the first departure airport during a duty period. For flights originating outside India, post-flight testing is required at the first Indian airport of landing.Being fit to fly is a regulatory requirement. But while the rules around alcohol have been in place for decades, psychoactive substances present a more complicated challenge.Drug testing is relatively new. The DGCA introduced the framework based on a 2019 report by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, which estimated that 2.8% of Indians had used cannabis in the previous year and 2.1% had used opioids. From 2019 to 2026, these numbers have only increased.These figures should not be taken as evidence that aviation personnel use drugs. Rather, they indicate the potential scale of the threat that the misuse of psychoactive substances can pose to aviation safety.The drug-testing system applies to flight crew and air traffic controllers. Testing is required before employment, following accidents, through random checks and as follow-up in previously confirmed cases.Random testing is currently designed to cover at least 10% of an organisation’s employees each year at specified airports. The testing panel is broad, covering substances including amphetamines, methamphetamines, cocaine, opioids, benzodiazepines, marijuana/hashish, MDMA and several others.The system is also designed around confirmation, rather than treating an initial screening result as conclusive. It is consequently more time- and resource-intensive than an alcohol test.A urine sample is divided into A and B portions. The initial screening is conducted under controlled conditions. If the A sample screens positive, the B sample is sent to a DGCA-authorised laboratory for confirmatory testing, with procedures in place to maintain the chain of custody.A person who returns a positive screening result is removed from safety-sensitive duties until the confirmatory report is received.If a first confirmed positive is established, the rules provide for de-addiction and rehabilitation, followed by repeat testing and clearance from a treating psychiatrist and the organisation’s chief medical officer before the person can return to active duty.A second confirmed positive, however, carries a far more severe consequence: cancellation of the licence.In other words, the regulatory system is built around two competing principles: aviation cannot afford to ignore substance use, but neither can it treat every initial test result as proof of impairment or permanently write off a person without due process.TOI spoke to aviation personnel to understand their perspective on the DGCA rules governing substance use in the industry.A senior pilot lauded the system, saying the DGCA maintains strict standards to protect the safety of the countless passengers who entrust their lives to the aviation system every day. But he said the responsibility does not rest with the regulator alone. A moral responsibility also falls on the crew entrusted with those lives.“The number of variables when it comes to substances in the market has increased and having access to them has become easier, but that does not mean that it can be used as an excuse. A soldier at the border is stressed too, but he has a responsibility to his nation to do his duty properly and honestly. So do we,” the pilot, who did not wish to be named, said.A cabin crew member, meanwhile, said drinking after work and, in some cases, using substances is not unheard of among crew. But she said there is a clear boundary between what happens off duty and the responsibilities that come with being in the air, and that most crew understand the implications of bringing such behaviour into the workplace.At the same time, she pointed to the pressures that come with the job.“I have been grounded for acne, for weight gain, I was once even grounded because my nails were too long,” she said.For cabin crew, the demands of the job extend beyond safety procedures and passenger service. Strict appearance standards, long and irregular working hours and constant interaction with passengers can add to the pressures of a profession in which employees are expected to maintain a high standard of presentation and hospitality at all times.These pressures, however, are difficult to separate from the broader conversation around substance use.It is this tension that sits at the heart of the debate. The pressures of the job are real, and an environment that leaves people constantly stressed can create conditions in which some may turn to alcohol or other substances. But for those sitting in the cockpit, stress cannot become an explanation for abandoning the responsibility that comes with the job.The Phuket incident has already prompted the regulator to widen that net.The DGCA has directed Indian airlines to conduct a one-time psychoactive-substance test on all their pilots by July 2027. The exercise will cover the country’s nearly 14,000 airline pilots. Air India had already begun its own one-time testing programme for about 5,000 pilots across Air India and Air India Express following the August 4 incident.The move comes as the DGCA works on a revision of its existing rules governing psychoactive-substance testing. The current framework requires random testing, with organisations expected to cover at least 10% of their employees annually. The proposed changes are expected to make the system more stringent.The senior pilot said the next step could also involve newer testing methods capable of delivering conclusive results faster, allowing airlines to test a much larger pool of crew rather than relying primarily on periodic random checks.The DGCA can test, regulate and punish. Airlines can monitor and intervene. But ultimately, the last line of defence is also the person sitting in the cockpit.
Article Summary: Air india a320 suddenly climbed 372 feet before dropping nearly 300 feet. Twenty-four people on board, including passengers and crew, were injured. Both pilots underwent the mandatory psychoactive-substance test after arriving in delhi, a requirement for flights originating outside india.

New Delhi: PM Narendra Modi held 15 formal bilateral meetings with heads of govt and state on the margins of Brics summit over three days, apart from pull-aside meetings with leaders of global institutions. On the closing day, Modi met leaders from Kazakhstan, South Africa, Philippines, Nigeria, Uganda and Burundi, the current chair of the African Union.In the meeting with Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the leaders reviewed bilateral cooperation in fields including trade, defence and security, connectivity, energy, critical minerals, emerging tech, creative economy and people-to-people ties.In his meeting with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos, Modi agreed to further deepen and expand collaboration in defence and security, trade and investment, space, railway infrastructure, fintech, education, tourism, science and technology, innovation and people-to-people ties."Both leaders agreed to advance relations under the aegis of the Strategic Partnership established between the two countries in August 2025 during the State Visit of President Marcos to India.PM welcomed the Philippines' decision to join the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure," said an Indian readout.Modi also held a bilateral meeting with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, recalling the successful translocation of cheetahs from South Africa to India and inviting South Africa to join the International Big Cat Alliance. The PM met Burundi President Evariste Ndayishimiye, chair of African Union, and discussed the early convening of 4th India-Africa Forum Summit.In another bilateral meeting with Nigerian Vice President Kashim Shettima Mustapha, the leaders focused on expanding cooperation in trade and investment, defence and security, energy, agriculture, health and digital technologies.In the meeting with Uganda Vice President Jessica Rose Epel Alupo, the focus was on tech partnerships, capacity building, knowledge sharing, investment facilitation and private-sector collaboration. New Delhi: PM Modi keeps a rather busy schedule at global events and it was no different as New Delhi hosted the Brics summit, with his schedule chock-a-block as he held 15 sit-down bilateral and numerous pull-aside meetings over three days since Friday.And, it was not only about numbers, but also India's success in having the grouping of 11 countries, some of whom like Iran and the UAE having deeply adversarial positions on the West Asia conflict, to sign on to a joint declaration affirmed.Modi's key bilateral meetings included those with presidents Xi Jinping (China), Vladimir Putin (Russia) and Masoud Pezeshkian (Iran).PM had the hard task of reconciling the conflicting takes of different countries - some like Russia and Iran are avowedly anti-West and some others, including India, do not want Brics to be pitted as a counteract against the West, and the wordings of joint declaration served the Indian interest well.If the participation from the likes of Xi Jinping, Putin and, not the least, Pezeshkian ensured that the summit had the heft and standing to draw the global attention to its goings-on, its successful conclusion reiterated the resonance of Indian policy of multi-alignment under Modi.Officials said that the fact that both Pezeshkian and UAE crown prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan shared a level of trust and comfort with Modi was telling.As the summit ended, the PM posted on social media, "Thank you to all Brics leaders for making the Delhi Summit very productive and outcome oriented!"

New Delhi: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called on Brics members to expand trade in national currencies to reduce dependence on existing financial and trade systems, as he slammed the West for imposing unilateral sanctions and for "crimes and genocide" against people of Iran and Gaza.With Iran bearing the brunt of sanctions, which have worsened the precarious condition of Iran's economy, Pezeshkian said at the concluding session of Brics summit that excessive dependence on financial and trade systems has made emerging economies vulnerable to political shocks.The latest round of sanctions has sharply eroded the value of the Iranian rial, aggravated the already high inflation and made oil exports, the main source of revenue, too prohibitive.He said sanctions are affecting global food security and people's welfare.Pezeshkian pitched for expanding trade in national currencies and strengthening the New Development Bank to enhance the economic resilience of Brics members. He said Brics had evolved beyond a framework for cooperation among emerging economies and had become a manifestation of growing demand for a more balanced and inclusive world in which "no centre of power has the right to determine the destiny of others".Brics now must play a greater role in building a more balanced, inclusive and just international order, the Iranian president said, stressing that resilience, cooperation and sustainability should be translated into action.

NEW DELHI: Russian President Vladimir Putin Sunday proposed a new insurance mechanism and a collaborative initiative for the grain market among Brics nations and called on the grouping to adopt a comprehensive approach to global challenges.He sought to assure members of the grouping that they have it in them to operate independently of the West-dominated trade systems. "We have independent routes for moving capital, labour and technologies. In fact, we can operate regardless of outside pressure. We have some promising initiatives going forward, such as creating an insurance mechanism and a grain market. These are Russian proposals, and we invite all other member states to make use of them. "His emphasis on Brics countries having their own insurance mechanism has come amid sanctions on ships exporting crude and grains from Russia. Insurance costs have risen, and the "shadow fleet "engaged by Russia to sell its products abroad is finding it difficult to operate.Read alongside the speeches of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the second day of the summit, Putin's pitch reflected the strong push from powerful Brics members to break away from the West-dominated system and build an alternative.They attested to efforts India made by seeking to prevent the grouping from turning into an anti-West bloc under its presidency.Grain exports from Russia, the world's largest wheat producer, have taken a big hit from Ukraine's drones. "Global South nations must jointly advance a better (global) governance structure and tackle both traditional and non-traditional security threats," Putin said. The Russian president also said Brics' global stature is rising as it focuses on charting an independent course to combat pressing global challenges.
Article Summary: Russian president vladimir putin has proposed a new insurance mechanism and a collaborative initiative for the grain market. He sought to assure members of the grouping that they have it in them to operate independently of the west-dominated trade systems.

New Delhi: Chinese President Xi Jinping Sunday proposed a five-point action plan, including an "open source and inclusive AI" initiative, along with digital industry and trade and investment facilitation as he urged Brics members to cooperate for a stable supply chain and a large integrated market.Also, urging Brics to rally the Global South and act as an active, stabilising and positive force amid changes not witnessed in a century, he said a world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed."President Xi stressed that Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, safeguard the basic norms of international relations, including sovereign equality, noninterference in internal affairs and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and ensure that international law and international rules are applied to all, free from double standards," said a statement issued by Chinese foreign ministry after his address at the second session of the Brics conference.Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the UN, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and see to it that reform of WTO proceeds in the right direction. The international financial architecture must be reformed and improved to increase the representation and voice of developing countries,” it said.Citing the current volatility in a multipolar world, Xi said, “To bring stability to the world and make it a better place, Brics countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, be an active, stabilising and positive force in international affairs, and advance the well-being of all humanity.”He then went on to elaborate on his economic agenda, arguing cooperation among members of the 11-nation bloc must be strengthened.As part of the AI initiative, Xi suggested China establish a Brics AI open source community, support cooperation in developing and applying large language models and build an open ecosystem.He also said China will push for establishing a Brics digital ecosystem cloud platform, hold skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment as part of plan on digital economy.“China proposes to establish a Brics special economic zone partnership, under which countries can set up an intelligent portal, coordinate policies, and build a new frontier for open development. In an effort to cultivate new drivers of economic and trade cooperation, China will hold the Brics Forum on Trade in Services next year,” he said on the trade and investment facilitation initiative.Besides, Xi offered his country’s assistance in building smart factories and developing standards and norms, with China looking to set up an engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards.“China will launch a Brics youth exchange programme for scientific and technological innovation, so as to cultivate more high-calibre talent,” he was quoted as saying in the statement.
Article Summary: Chinese president xi jinping hailed brics as an influential cooperation platform. He urged brics members to cooperate for a stable supply chain and a large integrated market. As part of the ai initiative, xi suggested china establish a brics ai open source community.
